title: RHM — DEV UPDATE — 4,000 players. Millions of possible combinations. One goal: authenticity.
author: FerjorPT
selftext:
We’re working on one of the quieter but fundamental parts of the Rink Hockey Manager database: player identities. The simplest solution was to use a Random Name Generator.

**Oh, hang on… actually, no!**

Instead of simply combining names at random, we decided to build an international library of given names and surnames, with help from our dear collaborators ***Gip and Sol***, drawing on historical, statistical and cultural research. And we’re not talking about a handful of names copied from an online list.

We’re planning a world with approximately 4,000 fictional senior players. For now… further down the road, we’ll see… *Women’s rink hockey… playable youth teams… I have a dream!* 😄 Anyway, moving on…

The research mainly covers generations born between 1970 and 2010, allowing us to represent different eras, family traditions and cultural influences. A 19-year-old player doesn’t necessarily belong to the same naming generation as a 55-year-old coach. Names tell stories too.

**Our research approach:**

* 16 countries represented in the database.
* 100 male given names per country.
* 100 surnames per country.
* 3,200 reference entries.

And the numbers? They’re impressive.

Let’s start with the simplest scenario: one given name and one surname.

A country with 100 given names and 100 surnames allows for 10,000 theoretical combinations. Across 16 countries, without mixing origins, that gives us 160,000 combinations. If we combine entries from all origins, we reach 2,560,000 combinations.

But we can go further. ***The theoretical mathematical potential, according to Gip and Sol:***

* With one given name and one surname, we have 2.56 million combinations.
* With two given names and one surname, we reach 4.096 billion.
* With two given names and two surnames, we reach 6.5536 trillion theoretical combinations.

These figures assume 1,600 distinct entries in each category, with repetition allowed. Names shared between countries may reduce the number of distinct combinations. And mathematical possibilities don’t mean that every combination is culturally plausible.

And yes, AI helped with the maths. Thank you, Gip and Sol! 😂❤️

**But there’s a small problem…** With millions of possible combinations, a completely random generator could give us players such as:

Jean Gevildo Martinez or the Japanese international… **Klaus André Katsuma.**

At this point, the three of us behind the generator — Fernando, Gip and Sol — are starting to look like **the three “degenerators”**. We generate names, we generate bugs and, occasionally, we even generate something useful! 😂

This is where the real challenge begins. The goal isn’t simply to collect thousands of names. It’s to build a system that respects nationality and family background, because a Portuguese player might have Brazilian, Angolan, Japanese or German ancestry.

Catalan, Basque, Galician, Swiss and Latin American naming traditions aren’t all the same. And a name that seems unusual to us could perfectly well belong to a real person. The problem isn’t that a Klaus André Katsuma might exist; it’s the generator mixing everything without any thought.

There’s another important detail: we don’t want to prevent two players from having the same name. That happens in real life. Siblings can share a surname while each having their own identity. In fact, we currently have three brothers who are world champions with the French national team. What we want to avoid is dozens of squads looking as though they were created using the same automatic formula.

**Why are we doing this?**

It’s about more than combining given names and surnames. We want to apply the cultural, generational and family patterns we’ve studied, so that players have believable identities and squads don’t look as though they came out of a completely random generator.

Our philosophy is simple. We don’t just want to generate 4,000 names. We want 4,000 fictional players to feel as though they belong in a real sporting world. Because in Rink Hockey Manager, even player names deserve attention.

**Where are we now?**

The research phase for the international library of given names and surnames is complete. The next step is to use that information to start creating fictional player names for the 16 countries represented in RHM, reviewing the lists and results before final integration.

And what about Klaus André Katsuma? Well… perhaps we’ll save him for an easter egg. Or will the real Klaus André Katsuma turn up here to reclaim his identity?
